title: Ikkyu
hook: the wild Zen poet-monk who mocked pomp

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nichiren, and a whole sutra held in its title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Your line: the title of the Lotus. What title did you catch holding more than it seemed? Day one thousand one.

A Zen monk walks through town in shabby robes, and people say he drinks in taverns and writes poems that would make an abbot blush. He calls himself Crazy Cloud. Stories say that when his teacher offered him the certificate that proves a student's awakening, he wouldn't keep it. Another story has him at New Year, when everyone is celebrating, carrying a skull on a stick through the streets as a reminder. Not all of these tales can be checked. But they all point the same way. Today, the wild monk, Ikkyu.
screen: `SHABBY ROBES, TAVERN POEMS.` → `NO CERTIFICATE.` → `A SKULL AT NEW YEAR.`

segments.voice: Ikkyu was a Japanese Rinzai Zen monk and poet. His poems were gathered in a collection known in English as the Crazy Cloud Anthology, and through them, more than through any sermon, he is remembered. First, what he aimed at. In his poems Ikkyu jabs at monks who wear fine robes, collect titles, sell certificates of awakening and run temples like businesses. For him, all that ceremony could become a costume over an empty room. Zen was supposed to strip things down to the plain truth, and here it was dressing up. Second, how he aimed. Not with a treatise, but with laughter, scandal and verse. His poems talk openly about wine, love and the body, things a respectable monk was supposed to keep quiet about. Readers argue about how literally to take them. Some hear a monk refusing to pretend he's purer than he is. Others hear a teacher using shock the way a Zen master uses a shout, to knock a student loose. Third, the twist. Tradition says that late in life Ikkyu was asked to lead the temple of Daitokuji, the kind of place he'd mocked, and he took up the work of rebuilding it. The wild monk didn't drop out of the tradition. He kept loving it enough to laugh at it. And that brings this week together. Eisai's tea, the old cook in the sun, Dogen's just sitting, forgetting the self and being-time, Nichiren's chant, and now Ikkyu's laugh. Each is its own path, but side by side they share a small thread: meet what's here, without the extras.
screen: `A POET-MONK: CRAZY CLOUD.` · `FINE ROBES, EMPTY ROOMS.` · `LAUGHTER, SCANDAL AND VERSE.` · `HE LOVED IT ENOUGH TO LAUGH.` · then, large: `DROP THE EXTRAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: laugh at one pomposity, and let it be your own. Sit easily. Let a few breaths settle. Then bring to mind one small way you dress yourself up: a title you like to mention, an opinion you defend a bit too loudly, the version of yourself you post. Look at it kindly, the way Ikkyu might, from a tavern doorway. Let a smile come if it wants to. You don't have to throw the thing away. Just see the costume as a costume. Then rest in whatever is under it, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Ikkyu. The Japanese Zen poet-monk who called himself Crazy Cloud and used laughter and verse to puncture pomp. Today's word.
Your line: the wild monk. Today, when you notice someone, or yourself, puffing up, let a quiet smile be your whole response. Day one thousand one.

howItsDone: Ikkyu is remembered in Japan through his poems, his calligraphy and folk stories, and Zen students and teachers read his verse as a reminder not to confuse the robes and ranks of practice with practice itself.
